text.Arrange blood tests, transport, medicine: Before each visit, check four things: the blood-test booking, how you will get there, your medicine supply and any help you need. Ask who will review the results and tell you whether the next dose can go ahead.
text.Keep the full handbook, three-page summa: Keep the handbook, short guide and treatment card in one place. Ask your team to fill in the real daytime and emergency numbers and print a replacement when the plan changes. A phone is optional.
text.Keep the pathology report, original mela: Record where the melanoma began, its pathology result and the sites involved now. This pathway treats melanoma that cannot be fully removed or has spread. Treatment after complete removal has a different aim and a separate plan.
text.A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether: The laboratory checks a sample of the melanoma for a BRAF V600 change. The result can identify a target for certain medicines. A change found in the tumour does not, by itself, establish an inherited condition.
text.Record the scans used to follow known di: Add planned scans, any operation and any radiotherapy to the same calendar. Ask what each part is intended to achieve and which team arranges it.
text.Report a new lump, changing mole, persis: Tell your team about a changing mole, a persistent sore, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. Improvement in a known tumour does not explain a new problem elsewhere.
text.Know where and when bloods are taken, ho: Write down where blood samples are taken, who receives the results and how you obtain the next appointment or medicine supply. Request a printed plan if that is easier to use.
text.Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appet: Bring up difficulties with eating, sleep, pain, energy, work or caring for someone. The team can arrange symptom support while cancer treatment continues.
text.Keep meals and fluids manageable and fol: Choose food, fluids and movement that you can manage, within any personal restrictions. Ask for help early if you are losing weight, drinking less or finding everyday activity harder.
text.Tell the team about sexual symptoms, rel: You can request a private discussion about intimacy, sexual symptoms or relationships. Ask for help if the agreed pregnancy precautions are difficult to follow.
text.Ask about symptom control, psychological: Supportive care addresses symptoms and daily life during cancer treatment. Palliative care can be part of that support; accepting it does not mean you must stop anticancer treatment.
text.If helpful, bring a family member or sup: Choose whether to involve a relative or supporter and what may be shared with them. Ask for an interpreter or a different information format. Check that you can explain the next dose, tests and urgent-contact plan in your own words.
text.Keep consent information, the three-page: Keep the current treatment summary, medicine list, test plan and contact card together. Use the printed instructions when you need them; the QR code is an optional link to further information.
text.Record medicines and doses received, imp: Ask for a treatment summary showing what you received, important side effects, admissions, the last dose and the follow-up team. Share the current version with your GP and other clinicians.
text.Confirm the next blood test, scan and re: Before leaving, confirm the next test and review, how you will receive results and whom to call sooner. Keep those numbers available after treatment ends.
text.Vismodegib blocks a protein called Smoot: Vismodegib blocks Smoothened, a protein in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. Abnormal activity in this pathway can drive basal cell cancer. Blocking it can slow tumour growth, while effects on normal tissues help explain cramps, taste changes and hair loss.
text.Report falling intake, weight loss, pain: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.
text.Arrange dates, medicine supply, transpor: Plan blood tests, travel and medicine collection in advance. If you need an interpreter or someone to help at home, tell the team before the appointment.
text.Keep this complete handbook, the three-p: Ask for your latest schedule and contact details on paper. Replace old versions when treatment changes so everyone helping you uses the same plan.
text.Keep the biopsy result, original site, d: Basal cell carcinoma starts in the skin. It usually grows locally; spread to distant organs is uncommon. Your team assesses the affected area and whether surgery or radiotherapy can treat it.
text.The cited NCCP vismodegib pathway concer: Vismodegib is used in the advanced basal cell carcinoma settings specified in your treatment protocol. Ask the team to explain why this medicine is suitable and why an operation or radiotherapy alone is not the agreed option.
text.Record operations, margin results, recon: Record previous operations, radiotherapy and other treatment to the same area. These details help the team plan further treatment and interpret changes in the skin.
text.Tell the team if you have had many BCCs: Several basal cell cancers at a young age or a suggestive family history may warrant a genetics assessment. Gorlin syndrome is one possible inherited cause. Testing is selected for the person; it is not required for every skin cancer.
text.Changes in a lesion, pain or a wound may: The team may measure or photograph a visible lesion and examine deeper tissue or lymph nodes. Scans are used when they answer a specific question. A photograph alone cannot show the full extent of disease.
text.Record surgery, radiotherapy and other a: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.
text.Arrange medicine supply, transport, inte: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.
text.For each test, record its purpose, due d: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.
text.Tell the team early about nausea, taste: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.
text.Use shade, protective clothing, a hat an: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.
text.Ask how to examine your skin, scars and: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.
text.If useful, keep a dated photograph with: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.
text.Use the dressings and skin-care plan rec: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.
text.Ask what evidence applies to your diagno: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.
text.Discuss other suitable treatments, clini: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.
text.Tell the team about work, transport, car: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.
text.Ask someone on the team to check that yo: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.
text.Keep follow-up for the treated lesion an: Follow-up covers the treated area and the rest of your skin. The team chooses examinations and scans for your situation. Vismodegib pregnancy-prevention and donation restrictions continue for the periods listed in your safety plan after the final dose.
text.This handbook can be used without a phon: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.
text.A neuroendocrine tumour (NET) starts in: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.
text.Differentiation describes how the cells: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.
text.A low-grade NET can have spread, and a h: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.
text.A functioning NET causes a hormone-relat: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.
text.Keep the primary site, differentiation,: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.
text.Blood counts measure infection-fighting: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.
text.CT and MRI help show tumour size and whe: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.
text.The team may measure selected blood or u: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.
text.Ask whether you need fasting, a timed ur: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.
text.A heart ultrasound may be needed for par: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.
text.Use the passport to write each test, its: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.
text.Record your usual bowel pattern, flushin: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.
text.Depending on the tumour, excess hormones: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.
text.Somatostatin analogue injections and oth: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.
text.Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic o: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.
text.Ask whether the main aim is to slow grow: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.
text.Some people need surgery, hormone-contro: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.
text.Ask why this option suits your tumour si: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.
text.A trial can measure time before cancer w: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.
text.Agree when you will review symptoms, tes: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.
text.Tell the team about weight loss, poor ap: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.
text.Follow your individual fluid advice, esp: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.
text.Living with repeated tests and treatment: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.
text.Ask your nurse or social worker about tr: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.
text.Keep the printed schedule, medicine list: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.
text.What is my exact diagnosis and grade? Wh: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.
text.Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiati: Radiotherapy directs a planned dose of radiation to the tumour area. Radiation damages cellular DNA; planning aims to limit exposure of nearby healthy brain. The dose and treated area affect both benefit and side effects.
text.Keep steroids and seizure medicines on t: If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.
text.Ask a trusted person to help check the c: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.
text.Temozolomide crosses into the brain and: Temozolomide produces chemical damage in DNA. Cells unable to repair that damage may stop dividing or die. Blood-forming cells can also be affected, which explains the need for blood counts and infection precautions. Radiotherapy damages DNA in the planned treatment area. Its team explains the separate dose, skin care and effects on the brain.
text.Use your oncology unit’s written emergen: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.
text.Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral e: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. PJP-prevention medicine is required during temozolomide with radiotherapy in this NCCP regimen. Your team supplies the prescription and decides how long to continue, including if lymphocyte counts remain low. Do not stop it just because radiotherapy has finished. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.
text.Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.
text.Grade describes features linked to how a: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.
text.IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts o: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.
text.MGMT is involved in repairing certain DN: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.
text.Keep the biopsy or operation date, patho: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.
text.A full blood count checks infection-figh: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.
text.MRI is the main scan used to assess many: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.
text.After treatment, inflammation and other: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.
text.Write the next MRI date, what question i: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.
text.Use the passport to distinguish a test b: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.
text.Write down your usual headache, strength: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.
text.Use your oncology unit’s written emergen: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.
text.Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swe: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.
text.If prescribed, take seizure medicines on: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.
text.Ask your clinical team about driving, wo: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.
text.Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemoth: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.
text.Ask whether the aim is to control the tu: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.
text.Clinical trials describe groups of peopl: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.
text.Ask about appropriate clinical trials, s: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.
text.Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.
text.Tell the team about word-finding, attent: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.
text.Report poor appetite, weight change, vom: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.
text.Anxiety, low mood, changes in behaviour: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.
text.Ask the specialist nurse or social worke: Plan travel, time away from work, caring duties and help with appointments. A nurse or social worker can identify practical support; agree who can help with tablets if needed.
text.Supportive and palliative care can help: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.
text.Keep the printed schedule, current medic: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.
text.Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral e: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. The team reviews infection and PJP risk, especially with steroids, low lymphocytes or prolonged treatment. A separate prevention prescription may be needed; do not assume the mandatory concurrent-radiotherapy plan automatically applies to this five-day schedule. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.
text.Keep any prescribed seizure medicine and: Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on a separate plan from chemotherapy. Before vincristine, report new weakness, tingling, walking difficulty or constipation. Check new symptom medicines with the team.
text.Lomustine and procarbazine have moderate: Lomustine and procarbazine have moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Vincristine alone has minimal emetic risk. The team supplies a day-specific anti-sickness plan, including the procarbazine days, and a rescue plan. Vincristine can slow the bowel through its effect on nerves. Preventive laxatives are recommended in NCCP; follow the prescribed plan and report constipation early. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs urgent advice. Procarbazine has important interactions. Avoid alcohol during treatment and follow the pharmacist’s written food restrictions and advice about when restrictions end. Check all prescription, over-the-counter, herbal and supplement products before taking them. Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on a separate plan from chemotherapy. Before vincristine, report new weakness, tingling, walking difficulty or constipation. Check new symptom medicines with the team.
text.A BRAF V600 change can keep the cell-gro: Dabrafenib inhibits an altered BRAF protein that sends growth signals inside eligible melanoma cells. Trametinib blocks another step in that pathway. The tumour’s BRAF result is checked before selecting this treatment.
text.MEK carries growth signals further along: Trametinib inhibits MEK proteins, which pass growth signals onward inside cells. It is used with dabrafenib in this plan. Normal tissues can also be affected, so heart checks and prompt reporting of eye or breathing symptoms remain important.
text.The evidence discussion must match the d: Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.
text.The supplied NCCN patient guide is an ed: SACTCheck explanations use the open clinical and medicine sources collected at the end of this document.
text.Keep the pathology summary, original ski: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.
text.A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether: A BRAF V600 result identifies whether the targeted medicines in this plan can act on the tumour. Keep the laboratory result and date. A tumour change is not, on its own, evidence of an inherited condition.
text.Record what surgery removed and whether: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.
text.Stage describes the extent of melanoma a: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.
text.Continue to report a new or changing mol: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.
text.Follow-up depends on stage, treatment an: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.
text.Nivolumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can: Nivolumab prevents the PD-1 checkpoint from dampening T-cell activity. This can strengthen an immune attack on melanoma. It can also trigger inflammation in healthy organs, including after treatment has ended.
text.Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another checkp: Ipilimumab blocks the CTLA-4 checkpoint that limits T-cell activity. In this plan it is combined with nivolumab during induction. The stronger immune effect can also increase inflammation in healthy organs.
text.A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether: BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.
text.Encorafenib blocks the BRAF V600 growth: Encorafenib blocks altered BRAF signalling in eligible melanoma. Binimetinib acts at a different step in the same growth pathway. Each medicine retains its own dosing and safety instructions.
text.Binimetinib inhibits MEK in the cell-gro: Binimetinib inhibits MEK proteins in the growth-signalling pathway. Alongside effects on cancer cells, it can affect muscle, heart and retinal tissue. The prescribed blood and heart checks and prompt review of new eye symptoms help detect these effects.
text.Keep steroids and seizure medicines on t: Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on their own schedules. Ask about missed or vomited doses. Agree a bowel plan if other medicines cause constipation and check interactions before adding a medicine.
text.Agree who can help with transport, presc: Agree help with prescriptions, travel, calls and symptom notes if fatigue, memory, sight or weakness makes these difficult. Your preferences guide who is involved. Keep the printed plan and real urgent contacts together.
text.Ask the specialist nurse or social worke: Tell the nurse or social worker about travel, employment, finances and caring responsibilities. Arrange practical help with medicines or appointments if symptoms make those tasks difficult.
text.Cemiplimab blocks PD-1 signalling that c: Cemiplimab blocks the PD-1 immune checkpoint. This can help T cells recognise and attack skin squamous cell cancer, but increased immune activity can also inflame healthy organs.
text.This guide concerns cutaneous squamous c: This pathway is for squamous cell carcinoma starting in the skin. Squamous cancers that begin in an internal organ follow different pathways. Keep the original skin site, pathology date and any sites of recurrence or spread in your record.
text.The size, depth, site, growth pattern an: The team considers the tumour’s size, depth, site and involvement of nearby structures or nerves, along with recurrence and immune status. Ask which features affect your plan. A risk category is not a measurement of treatment response.
text.The cited NCCP cemiplimab setting is adv: This cemiplimab pathway applies when advanced skin squamous cell carcinoma cannot appropriately be treated with curative surgery or radiotherapy. Ask the team to record the treatment aim and why this option fits your situation.
text.Tell the oncology team about an organ tr: Tell the team about a transplant, autoimmune illness and all immune-suppressing medicines. These can alter the risks of immune treatment. Oncology and the relevant specialists need a shared plan; do not stop transplant medicines or steroids yourself.
text.A skin tumour or treatment can affect pa: Ask for help with wound care, pain, bleeding, eating, movement or sleep. Keep a contact for worsening bleeding, infection symptoms, new nerve pain or weakness. These changes need assessment rather than waiting for the next photograph.
text.Follow-up includes examination of the tr: Follow-up examines the treated area, other skin and relevant lymph nodes. The team adds scans or other specialist checks for your disease and symptoms. Keep wound care and skin surveillance in the same plan.
text.Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1, a signal that: Pembrolizumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint, allowing T cells to remain more active against cancer. Immune activity can also affect normal organs, so new symptoms matter during treatment and after it stops.
text.The NCCN patient reference supports educ: SACTCheck explanations use the open clinical and medicine sources collected at the end of this document.
text.Nivolumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can: Nivolumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint that restrains T cells. The resulting immune activity may control melanoma but can also inflame normal organs. Side effects may first appear after the final dose.
text.Follow individual instructions on distan: Before discharge, obtain a paper plan with the end date for each restriction on contact, sleeping, work, travel and body-fluid handling. First-week instructions include daily bathing, careful handwashing, sitting to pass urine and separately washing body-fluid-soiled laundry. Ask for specific advice about pads, incontinence or a catheter. Examples include sleeping separately from a partner for 14 days and from pregnant people or children for three weeks; restrictions differ by contact and circumstance. Your medical physicist sets your personal instructions. Tell them before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.
text.Carry the discharge letter and treatment: Carry the discharge letter and the official radiation-treatment card for the period the medical physicist specifies. They identify the treatment and date and help with travel, radiation detectors and other healthcare. The SACTCheck wallet card is an additional record and does not replace them. Tell healthcare staff about the treatment; radiation precautions must never delay urgent care.
text.The detailed treatment information descr: Radiation-assessment scans measure where the treatment went and the radiation delivered to organs. They answer a different question from CT or MRI scans of tumour response. The detailed treatment information describes three radiation scans on separate days in the first week after the first infusion, starting the next day, and one after later infusions; response CT or MRI is described between the second and third infusions and after the course. Confirm your actual bookings with the team: these are service arrangements, not a universal timetable for every neuroendocrine tumour.
text.NCCP specifies four-weekly blood tests f: Blood counts, kidney and liver tests continue every four weeks for at least three months after the last administration, then every three months for the following year. Your written discharge plan may also include two-weekly tests for the first eight weeks after the last infusion. The team confirms those extra early appointments and who reviews the results.
text.The team decides whether a delayed admin: Low blood counts, kidney or liver changes, other side effects or a change in the cancer may lead the specialist to postpone, reduce or stop treatment. A four-stamp record shows planned administrations, not medical clearance. A dose does not automatically become suitable at the maximum interval. Keep the blood-test and symptom plan while waiting for the team’s decision.

direct_language.Your Irish PRRT service plan in print: Your specialist treatment plan in print
direct_language.The current Irish eligibility and specia: Your specialist team confirms that the treatment criteria apply to you.
